title: How to know der, die, or das — German noun gender rules
summary: How do you know if a German noun is der, die, or das? Clear rules by noun ending, category, and exceptions — plus a trick for when you can't guess.
body:
How to know if a noun is der, die, or das

Rules for predicting German noun gender — and what to do when the rules don't apply.

Every German noun has a grammatical gender: masculine (der), feminine (die), or neuter (das). Gender controls articles, adjective endings, and pronouns, so guessing wrong changes a lot in one sentence. The honest answer up front: there is no single rule that covers every noun. But about 80% of nouns follow predictable patterns — learn those patterns and you'll guess correctly far more often than by chance.

Rule 1: by noun ending

Endings are the most reliable shortcut. These are near-universal:

EndingUsuallyExamples
-ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -ion, -tät, -ik, -urdie (feminine)die Zeitung, die Freiheit, die Universität
-e (most)die (feminine)die Lampe, die Blume, die Tasche
-chen, -leindas (neuter)das Mädchen, das Büchlein
-ment, -tum, -um, -madas (neuter)das Argument, das Datum, das Thema
-er (agent), -ling, -ich, -ig, -ismusder (masculine)der Lehrer, der Frühling, der Tourismus
-or, -ist, -ant, -entder (masculine)der Doktor, der Student, der Tourist

Rule 2: by meaning

Masculine (der)

  • Male people and animals: der Mann, der Vater, der Hund.
  • Days, months, seasons: der Montag, der Juli, der Winter.
  • Weather, directions, points of the compass: der Regen, der Norden.
  • Alcoholic drinks (with one famous exception, das Bier): der Wein.
  • Car brands: der BMW, der Audi.

Feminine (die)

  • Female people and animals: die Frau, die Mutter, die Katze.
  • Most numbers and ordinals as nouns: die Eins.
  • Most trees and flowers: die Eiche, die Rose.
  • Motorcycle and ship brands: die Harley, die Titanic.

Neuter (das)

  • Young creatures: das Kind, das Baby, das Kalb. (Yes, this is why das Mädchen is neuter.)
  • Metals and chemical elements: das Gold, das Eisen.
  • Infinitives used as nouns: das Schwimmen, das Lesen.
  • Most colors and languages as nouns: das Rot, das Deutsch.

Rule 3: compound nouns take the last noun's gender

Compounds are easy: the final noun decides the article. die Tür + der Schlüssel = der Türschlüssel. If you know the simple noun, you know the compound.

What to do when you can't guess

When the ending doesn't help and the meaning doesn't fit any category, there's no shortcut — you have to learn the article with the noun. A few habits that work:

  • Always write new vocabulary as article + noun + plural: die Tür, -en, not just Tür.
  • Read the article out loud every time. After a few weeks the wrong article starts sounding wrong.
  • When you read a new sentence and aren't sure about a word's gender, check it — don't let a guess become a habit.

title: Haben or sein in German Perfekt? — rules + list
summary: When to use haben and when to use sein as the auxiliary verb for the German Perfekt. Clear rules, common verbs with sein, and tricky cases like fahren and fliegen.
body:
Haben or sein as auxiliary?

How to choose the right helping verb for the German Perfekt.

German uses the perfect tense (Perfekt) for almost all spoken past actions. Its formula is simple: auxiliary verb + Partizip II. The only question is whether the auxiliary should be haben or sein. Most verbs take haben. A smaller group takes sein.

Default rule: haben

Use haben unless the verb meets a specific condition that requires sein.

  • Ich habe ein Buch gelesen.
  • Sie hat Kaffee getrunken.
  • Wir haben im Park gespielt.

Use sein if the verb meets any of these

  1. Movement from A to B — the subject goes somewhere.
    Ich bin nach Berlin gefahren. Sie ist nach Hause gegangen.
  2. Change of state — the subject becomes something different.
    Der Baum ist gewachsen. Das Kind ist eingeschlafen. Das Eis ist geschmolzen.
  3. These three verbs, always: sein (to be), bleiben (to stay), werden (to become).
    Ich bin müde gewesen. Er ist Arzt geworden.

Common sein-verbs to memorize

VerbPartizip IIMeaning
gehengegangento go
kommengekommento come
fahrengefahrento drive / travel
fliegengeflogento fly
laufengelaufento run
reisengereistto travel
schwimmengeschwommento swim
springengesprungento jump
steigengestiegento climb / rise
sterbengestorbento die
wachsengewachsento grow
aufstehenaufgestandento get up
einschlafeneingeschlafento fall asleep
passierenpassiertto happen
bleibengebliebento stay
seingewesento be
werdengewordento become

The tricky case: fahren, fliegen, schwimmen

Verbs of motion normally take sein, but if you use them transitively — with a direct object — they flip to haben.

  • Ich bin nach Italien geflogen. (I flew to Italy — motion, sein)
  • Der Pilot hat die Maschine geflogen. (The pilot flew the plane — transitive, haben)
  • Sie ist über den See geschwommen. (movement, sein)
  • Sie hat eine neue Technik geschwommen. (transitive, haben — rare but correct)

Austrian and Swiss usage

In southern German, Austrian, and Swiss usage, sitzen, stehen, and liegen often take sein. In standard northern German, they take haben. Both are accepted.

title: The four German cases explained — nominative, accusative, dative, genitive
summary: A clear overview of the four German cases with article tables, typical uses, and example sentences. Understand nominative, accusative, dative, and genitive in one page.
body:
The four German cases explained

Nominative, accusative, dative, genitive — what each one does and how to spot it.

German marks the role of a noun in a sentence using case. Instead of relying on word order (as English does), German changes the articles and some endings. There are four cases: nominative, accusative, dative, and genitive. Learning them is the single biggest investment that pays off in every German sentence you read or write.

Definite article table

Casemascfemneutplural
Nominativederdiedasdie
Accusativedendiedasdie
Dativedemderdemden (+n)
Genitivedes (+s)derdes (+s)der

Nominative — the subject

The nominative is the "who is doing the action" case. It's the form you find in a dictionary.

  • Der Hund schläft. — the dog is the subject.
  • Also used after sein, werden, bleiben: Das ist ein Student.

Accusative — the direct object

The accusative marks the thing being directly acted on.

  • Ich sehe den Mann. — den Mann is what I see.
  • Always after these prepositions: durch, für, gegen, ohne, um.
  • After two-way prepositions when there's motion toward a destination.

Dative — the indirect object

The dative marks the recipient — "to whom" or "for whom" something happens.

  • Ich gebe dem Kind einen Apfel. — dem Kind is the recipient.
  • Always after these prepositions: aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu, gegenüber.
  • After two-way prepositions when describing static location.
  • With dative-only verbs: helfen, danken, folgen, gefallen, gehören, antworten, etc.
  • Plural nouns add an -n in dative if they don't already end in -n or -s: mit den Kindern.

Genitive — possession and formal prepositions

Genitive expresses possession or relationship. It's slightly formal; spoken German often replaces it with von + dative.

  • Das Auto meines Vaters. — my father's car.
  • Masculine and neuter singular nouns add -s or -es: des Mannes, des Hauses.
  • Genitive prepositions: (an)statt, trotz, während, wegen, außerhalb, innerhalb.
  • In conversation, wegen dem Regen is common (dative); in writing, wegen des Regens is standard.

How to identify a case in a sentence

  1. Find the verb. Is it a dative-only verb? If yes, its object is dative.
  2. Find a preposition. If it's in a fixed accusative or dative list, the case is decided.
  3. Otherwise, ask wer?/was? → nominative. wen?/was? → accusative. wem? → dative.

title: Accusative vs dative in German — simple guide with examples
summary: The clearest way to tell accusative from dative in German: who vs whom, article endings, dative-only verbs, two-way prepositions, and worked examples.
body:
Accusative vs dative in German

The core idea, the article endings, the verbs that break the pattern, and worked examples.

The core idea in one line

Accusative = the direct object (the thing being acted on). Dative = the indirect object (the recipient / the one affected).

English uses word order for this. German uses case. Compare:

  • I give the man the book. → Ich gebe dem Mann das Buch.
  • dem Mann = dative (the recipient). das Buch = accusative (the thing given).

Ask two questions:

  1. Wen/was? (Whom/what [is acted on]?) → accusative.
  2. Wem? (To/for whom?) → dative.

Article endings — the thing to memorize

Casemascfemneutplural
Nominativederdiedasdie
Accusativedendiedasdie
Dativedemderdemden (+n on noun)

Notice the shortcut: only the masculine noun changes in accusative (der → den). The dative changes everything. That's why masculine nouns are where most learners get stuck first.

Indefinite articles follow the same pattern: ein/eine/ein → einen/eine/ein (acc) and einem/einer/einem (dat).

Verbs that force dative

Some verbs always take a dative object even though English treats them as direct. Memorize these — they're the most common cause of mistakes:

  • helfen — Ich helfe dir. (not dich)
  • danken — Ich danke dem Lehrer.
  • antworten — Sie antwortet mir.
  • folgen — Der Hund folgt dem Mann.
  • gefallen — Das Buch gefällt mir.
  • gehören — Das Auto gehört meinem Bruder.
  • glauben (to a person) — Ich glaube dir.
  • passen, schmecken, fehlen, begegnen

Prepositions fix the case

Some prepositions always take accusative (durch, für, gegen, ohne, um), some always dative (aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu), and the two-way prepositions (in, an, auf, über, unter, vor, hinter, neben, zwischen) switch based on motion vs location. See the two-way prepositions guide.

Motion vs location test

  • Ich gehe in die Schule. (motion → accusative)
  • Ich bin in der Schule. (location → dative)

Worked examples

Er gibt seiner Schwester einen Brief. — seiner Schwester dative (recipient), einen Brief accusative (object given).

Sie hilft dem alten Mann. — dative because helfen is a dative verb.

Wir legen das Buch auf den Tisch. — accusative because there's motion onto the table.

Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch. — dative because it's a static location.

title: German two-way prepositions (Wechselpräpositionen) — accusative vs dative
summary: The nine German Wechselpräpositionen (in, an, auf, über, unter, vor, hinter, neben, zwischen) and how to choose accusative or dative — motion vs location, with examples.
body:
German two-way prepositions (Wechselpräpositionen)

Nine prepositions that can take accusative or dative. Here's how to pick the right one.

German has nine "two-way" prepositions — called Wechselpräpositionen — that can govern either the accusative or the dative case. The choice depends on whether the verb describes motion toward a new location (accusative) or a static location or motion within a space (dative).

The nine Wechselpräpositionen

PrepositionMeaning
inin, into
anat, on (vertical surface), to
aufon (horizontal surface), onto
überover, above, across
unterunder, below
vorin front of, before
hinterbehind
nebennext to, beside
zwischenbetween

The rule: Wohin? vs. Wo?

Ask a test question:

  • Wohin? (Where to?) → motion into a new place → accusative.
  • Wo? (Where?) → static position or motion within a fixed area → dative.

Side-by-side examples

Accusative (Wohin?)Dative (Wo?)
Ich gehe in die Küche.Ich bin in der Küche.
Sie hängt das Bild an die Wand.Das Bild hängt an der Wand.
Er legt das Buch auf den Tisch.Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch.
Der Vogel fliegt über den Fluss.Die Lampe hängt über dem Tisch.
Die Katze kriecht unter das Bett.Die Katze schläft unter dem Bett.
Ich stelle das Fahrrad vor das Haus.Das Fahrrad steht vor dem Haus.
Er geht hinter das Gebäude.Er wartet hinter dem Gebäude.
Sie setzt sich neben ihn.Sie sitzt neben ihm.
Er stellt die Vase zwischen die Bücher.Die Vase steht zwischen den Büchern.

Two very useful verb pairs

German distinguishes placement (accusative, motion) from position (dative, state). These pairs come up all the time:

  • stellen (to put, upright) vs. stehen (to stand)
  • legen (to put, lying) vs. liegen (to lie)
  • setzen (to set/sit down) vs. sitzen (to sit)
  • hängen (to hang — transitive/accusative) vs. hängen (to hang — intransitive/dative)

If the verb is from the left column (placement), you're heading into a new position → accusative. Right column verbs describe state → dative.

Common contractions

  • in das → ins — ich gehe ins Kino
  • in dem → im — ich bin im Kino
  • an das → ans
  • an dem → am
  • auf das → aufs (informal)

When motion verbs still take dative

Watch out: a verb of motion that describes movement within a place (not toward a new one) takes dative.

  • Ich laufe im Park. (I run around inside the park — dative)
  • Ich laufe in den Park. (I'm running into the park from outside — accusative)

title: Partizip II in German — how to form it + common list
summary: How to form Partizip II for weak, strong, and mixed verbs in German, with a practical list of common irregular past participles and when to use ge-.
body:
Partizip II: how to form the German past participle

Rules for weak, strong, and mixed verbs, plus a list of common irregulars.

Partizip II (the past participle) is what you need to build the perfect tense (Perfekt), the pluperfect (Plusquamperfekt), the passive, and many adjectives. Most German conversations about the past use Perfekt, so this form is everywhere.

Weak verbs — regular pattern

Weak verbs (the vast majority) form Partizip II with ge- + stem + -t.

  • machen → gemacht
  • lernen → gelernt
  • kaufen → gekauft
  • arbeiten → gearbeitet (stems ending in -t, -d add -et)

Strong verbs — vowel change + -en

Strong verbs change their stem vowel and end in -en.

  • singen → gesungen
  • schreiben → geschrieben
  • fahren → gefahren
  • gehen → gegangen

There's no shortcut — you memorize strong verbs one by one. See the strong verb list.

Mixed verbs — vowel change + -t

A small group mixes both: stem change plus -t ending.

  • bringen → gebracht
  • denken → gedacht
  • kennen → gekannt
  • wissen → gewusst

When the "ge-" prefix is dropped

Two rules cancel the ge-:

  1. Verbs ending in -ieren: studieren → studiert, telefonieren → telefoniert.
  2. Verbs with inseparable prefixes (be-, emp-, ent-, er-, ge-, ver-, zer-, miss-): bekommen → bekommen, verstehen → verstanden, erzählen → erzählt.

Separable-prefix verbs

With separable prefixes, ge- goes between the prefix and the stem.

  • aufmachen → aufgemacht
  • ankommen → angekommen
  • einkaufen → eingekauft

Common irregular Partizip II forms

InfinitivePartizip IIAuxiliary
seingewesensein
habengehabthaben
werdengewordensein
gehengegangensein
kommengekommensein
fahrengefahrensein
essengegessenhaben
trinkengetrunkenhaben
sehengesehenhaben
lesengelesenhaben
schreibengeschriebenhaben
sprechengesprochenhaben
nehmengenommenhaben
findengefundenhaben
gebengegebenhaben
bleibengebliebensein
stehengestandenhaben
verstehenverstandenhaben

title: German plural rules — five endings and how to predict them
summary: How to form German plurals: the five plural endings, which ending goes with which gender, umlaut rules, and common exceptions. A practical shortcut that covers most nouns.
body:
German plural rules

Five endings, five patterns. Plus how to predict which noun uses which.

German has five main plural endings: -n/-en, -e, -er, -s, and no ending at all. Some also add an umlaut (ä, ö, ü) on the stem vowel. There's no single rule, but noun gender and ending make most plurals predictable. In the plural, every article is die, regardless of the singular gender.

The five endings at a glance

EndingTypical nounsExamples
-n / -enmost feminine nounsdie Frau → Frauen, die Blume → Blumen, die Zeitung → Zeitungen
-e (± umlaut)many masculine and some neuterder Tag → Tage, der Stuhl → Stühle, das Jahr → Jahre
-er (+ umlaut if possible)many one-syllable neuter nounsdas Kind → Kinder, das Haus → Häuser, das Buch → Bücher
-sforeign/loan words, words ending in a voweldas Auto → Autos, das Hotel → Hotels, der Park → Parks
no ending (± umlaut)masc/neut ending in -er, -en, -el, -chen, -leinder Lehrer → Lehrer, der Vater → Väter, das Mädchen → Mädchen

Patterns by gender

Feminine nouns

~90% take -(e)n. Almost automatic.

  • die Lampe → Lampen, die Tasche → Taschen, die Universität → Universitäten
  • Exceptions with umlaut + -e: die Hand → Hände, die Stadt → Städte, die Maus → Mäuse.

Masculine nouns

Most take -e, often with umlaut.

  • der Hund → Hunde, der Zug → Züge, der Arzt → Ärzte
  • Those ending in -er, -en, -el usually take no ending (maybe umlaut): der Bruder → Brüder, der Wagen → Wagen, der Apfel → Äpfel.
  • "Weak" masculines add -(e)n: der Junge → Jungen, der Student → Studenten.

Neuter nouns

No single rule, but:

  • One-syllable neuter nouns often take -er with umlaut: das Kind → Kinder, das Buch → Bücher.
  • Neuter nouns ending in -chen or -lein never change: das Mädchen → Mädchen.
  • Loan words take -s: das Auto → Autos.

Dative plural rule

In the dative plural, the noun adds an -n if it doesn't already end in -n or -s.

  • die Kinder → mit den Kindern
  • die Bücher → in den Büchern
  • die Autos → mit den Autos (no change, ends in -s)

Learn the plural with the noun

The best habit is to learn every new noun with its article and its plural: die Hand, die Hände. Writing vocabulary as three items (article, noun, plural) means you never have to reconstruct the plural from guesses.

title: German word order (Satzbau) — V2, subordinate clauses, TeKaMoLo
summary: German word order in main and subordinate clauses: the verb-second rule, verb-final in dependent clauses, and the TeKaMoLo order for time, cause, manner, place.
body:
German word order (Satzbau)

The three rules that cover 95% of German sentences.

German word order feels unpredictable at first, but it's governed by a small number of rules. The most important one is that the conjugated verb must be the second element in a main clause — almost always. Once you internalize this, German sentences start clicking into place.

Rule 1: V2 — the verb is always second in a main clause

The conjugated verb occupies the second "position" (not necessarily the second word — the second unit).

  • Ich gehe heute ins Kino. (Ich / gehe / heute / ins Kino)
  • Heute gehe ich ins Kino. (Heute / gehe / ich / ins Kino)
  • Ins Kino gehe ich heute. (Ins Kino / gehe / ich / heute)

The fronted element changes emphasis but the verb stays in position 2. You can move anything to the front, but the verb won't budge.

Rule 2: subordinate clauses send the verb to the end

After subordinating conjunctions like weil, dass, wenn, obwohl, als, während, damit, ob, the conjugated verb goes to the very end.

  • Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich krank bin.
  • Ich weiß, dass du Recht hast.
  • Wenn es regnet, nehme ich einen Regenschirm. (wenn-clause first → main clause starts with the verb to keep V2 globally)

Rule 3: in Perfekt/modal/future, the non-finite verb goes to the end

When the sentence has more than one verb (auxiliary + participle, or modal + infinitive), the conjugated verb is in position 2 and the other verb goes to the end.

  • Ich habe gestern ein Buch gelesen.
  • Er will morgen nach Berlin fahren.
  • Wir werden nächste Woche unseren Freund besuchen.

This is called the Satzklammer (sentence bracket): the verbs form a frame around the rest of the clause.

TeKaMoLo — the order of adverbial info

When a sentence has several adverbials (time, cause, manner, place), German tends to put them in this order:

  • Temporal (when?)
  • Kausal (why?)
  • Modal (how?)
  • Lokal (where?)

Example: Ich fahre morgen (Te) wegen der Arbeit (Ka) mit dem Zug (Mo) nach München (Lo).

You can front one of these elements to emphasize it (then the verb still comes next, per V2), but their internal order stays TeKaMoLo.

Object order: dative before accusative (usually)

When both objects are nouns, dative comes first: Ich gebe dem Kind einen Apfel.

When one is a pronoun, the pronoun comes first: Ich gebe ihn (acc) dem Kind (dat).

Yes/no questions and commands

In yes/no questions and imperatives, the verb is in position 1:

  • Kommst du mit?
  • Geh nach Hause!

title: German modal verbs — können, müssen, dürfen, sollen, wollen, mögen
summary: Meaning, conjugation, and usage of the six German modal verbs: können, müssen, dürfen, sollen, wollen, mögen (and möchten). With example sentences and sentence structure.
body:
German modal verbs

Six verbs that change the meaning of another verb — ability, obligation, permission, desire.

German has six modal verbs: können, müssen, dürfen, sollen, wollen, mögen. They work alongside another verb (the infinitive) to express a mode — whether something is possible, required, allowed, expected, wanted, or liked. They're among the most common verbs in spoken German.

Meaning in one line each

  • können — can, to be able to
  • müssen — must, to have to
  • dürfen — to be allowed to
  • sollen — should, supposed to
  • wollen — to want to
  • mögen — to like (often used in its subjunctive form möchten = "would like")

Present tense conjugation

Modals have irregular singular forms (vowel change) but regular plural.

könnenmüssendürfensollenwollenmögen
ichkannmussdarfsollwillmag
dukannstmusstdarfstsollstwillstmagst
er/sie/eskannmussdarfsollwillmag
wirkönnenmüssendürfensollenwollenmögen
ihrkönntmüsstdürftsolltwolltmögt
sie/Siekönnenmüssendürfensollenwollenmögen

Sentence structure

The modal is the conjugated verb (position 2 in a main clause); the second verb goes to the end as an infinitive.

  • Ich kann Deutsch sprechen.
  • Du musst jetzt gehen.
  • Wir wollen morgen nach Berlin fahren.

Möchten vs. wollen

Möchten is the subjunctive of mögen and means "would like" — politer than wollen. In restaurants, shops, or polite requests, use möchten.

  • Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte. (polite)
  • Ich will einen Kaffee. (blunt, more like a demand)

Past tense: Präteritum is preferred

With modals, spoken German usually uses Präteritum, not Perfekt.

  • Ich konnte gestern nicht kommen. (rather than habe nicht kommen können)
  • Sie musste früh aufstehen.
  • Wir wollten ins Kino gehen.

Common meanings in context

  • Das kann sein. — That could be. (possibility)
  • Er muss krank sein. — He must be sick. (logical deduction)
  • Du darfst nicht rauchen. — You're not allowed to smoke.
  • Er soll sehr klug sein. — He's said to be very clever.
  • Ich mag Schokolade. — I like chocolate. (no second verb needed)

Related: German word order · Strong verbs

German strong & irregular verbs

The most common irregular verbs, grouped by vowel pattern.

Vowel-change patterns

Many strong verbs fall into predictable groups. Some of the bigger ones:

  • ei → ie → ie: bleiben–blieb–geblieben, schreiben–schrieb–geschrieben, steigen–stieg–gestiegen.
  • ie → o → o: fliegen–flog–geflogen, verlieren–verlor–verloren, schließen–schloss–geschlossen.
  • i → a → u: singen–sang–gesungen, trinken–trank–getrunken, finden–fand–gefunden.
  • e → a → o: sprechen–sprach–gesprochen, helfen–half–geholfen, nehmen–nahm–genommen.
  • e → a → e: essen–aß–gegessen, geben–gab–gegeben, lesen–las–gelesen.
